disease_info: Persistent Depressive Disorder (PDD), or dysthymia, is characterized by a chronically low mood lasting at least two years in adults, accompanied by other depressive features that are present more days than not. Individuals often describe it as a longstanding sense of gloom or joylessness rather than discrete mood episodes, and they may function outwardly while experiencing significant internal distress and reduced quality of life. The course is typically insidious and protracted, with onset often linked to enduring stressors or personality vulnerabilities rather than a single dramatic event. It is distinguished from major depressive disorder by its chronicity and generally milder but persistent symptoms, though the two can coexist when more severe episodes are superimposed on the chronic low mood.

narrative.personality: Larry is a highly creative, achievement‑driven technologist who juggles many artistic and social pursuits while maintaining a meticulous, disciplined approach to work and finances.
narrative.stressor: About two and a half years ago, Larry was promoted into a senior product leadership role just as his company began an aggressive restructuring, increasing his workload, responsibility for mentoring younger teams, and pressure to deliver ambitious releases on tight timelines. Initially he responded by throwing himself into work, staying late, cutting back on guitar, painting, and social activities, telling himself it was a temporary sprint that would pay off with stock options and recognition. As months turned into years, the relentless pace, constant context‑switching between strategic planning and hands‑on coding, and a series of under‑resourced launches left him feeling chronically depleted and detached from the creativity that had once energized him, yet he kept pushing to meet expectations and maintain his careful budget and future plans. Over time, he noticed that his nights were increasingly dominated by lying awake cycling through work problems and financial contingencies, and when this persistent pattern began eroding his performance and his enjoyment of even his favorite hobbies, he finally decided to seek psychiatric help at the urging of a colleague who noticed his ongoing struggle.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I can’t seem to sleep through the night anymore, and it’s been going on for years now.”

narrative.personality: Louise is a conscientious, detail‑oriented young woman who balances her logistics work with a reflective, artistic side and uses creative outlets and yoga to soothe her underlying anxiety.
narrative.stressor: Around two years and a few months ago, Louise’s hours at the warehouse became inconsistent after a shift reorganization, just as tuition and book costs for her business classes increased and her family was no longer able to help as much financially. She began picking up every extra shift she could, often working late nights and early mornings, while trying to keep up with coursework and telling herself that this grind was necessary to eventually move into a better‑paying supply‑chain role. As the financial pressure persisted, she started skipping regular meals to save money and relying on cheap, convenient food and late‑night coffee runs, gradually losing the structure of home‑cooked dinners, yoga classes, and choir rehearsals that had formerly anchored her week. When she realized that her eating patterns had become erratic, her weight had noticeably changed, and she no longer had the energy or motivation for painting, church, or studying the way she wanted—yet the money worries still felt unrelenting—she sought psychiatric care after a campus advisor suggested that something more than “just stress” might be going on.
narrative.chief_complaint: “My eating is all over the place and my weight’s been changing a lot these past couple years.”

narrative.personality: James is an outgoing, competitive young man who thrives on high‑energy social interactions and community involvement, but tends to approach life plans flexibly and somewhat disorganized.
narrative.stressor: Just over two years ago, James transitioned from the structure of high school and part‑time jobs into full‑time insurance sales, a role that promised high earnings but offered little stability and depended heavily on commissions and constant self‑promotion. At first he enjoyed the hustle—networking at community events, staying out late with coworkers, and chasing monthly sales targets—but as the novelty faded, the pressure to continually perform, manage adult responsibilities, and watch peers move on to college or more predictable careers left him feeling unmoored. Over time, he coped by leaning into an irregular lifestyle of skipped home meals, fast food between appointments, and late‑night socializing, gradually losing the balanced routines of sports, tutoring, and family dinners that had grounded him, even as his outward charm and drive at work continued. When he eventually noticed that his appetite and weight had shifted in a way that bothered him, and that the change seemed tied to a long‑standing sense of being worn down and off his game despite his ongoing social and work activity, he agreed to see a psychiatrist after his primary care doctor suggested a mental health evaluation.
narrative.chief_complaint: “My appetite and weight have really changed over the last couple of years, and I don’t feel like myself.”
